extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public (early-18th-century English readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical essays and moral/satirical pieces for a general public (The Spectator-style), mixing humour, social observation, and occasional political or religious reflection. Focuses on rhetorical devices, social norms, and moral judgement used in short topical essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipe-lighting as social overture
rubrics_metrics.description: "lighting a Man's Pipe at the same Candle, is looked upon among Brother-smokers as an Overture to Conversation and Friendship.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as social etiquette to initiate conversation and familiarity (anecdote: narrator lights his pipe at same candle and joins conversation in coffee-house).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of asterisks/dashes to avoid offence
rubrics_metrics.description: "he is very cautious of giving Offence, and has therefore put two Dashes into his Pudding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may substitute asterisks, dashes, or partial names to avoid explicit offence; this is presented as a deliberate stylistic device but attracts criticism from those who see it as cowardly or evasive (example: coffee-house disputants complain about asterisks and dashes representing great men).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission/blank (a 'Chasm') as modesty or evasiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: "he leaves a blank Space without so much as a Consonant to direct us?... a Chasm, that in my Opinion looks modest enough."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving blanks/omissions can be read as modesty or prudence, but critics may interpret the same device as an attempt to creep out of responsibility; the device functions rhetorically to hint without naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware 'overwise' readers who find innuendo everywhere
rubrics_metrics.description: "A Man who has a good Nose at an Innuendo, smells Treason and Sedition in the most innocent Words that can be put together..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary principle for writers: ambiguous or satirical remarks risk being misconstrued as personal satire or libel by those inclined to read innuendo; anecdote of marginal notes turning a moral book into an apparent local libel illustrates the anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak plainly for the public good and refuse to flatter ill men
rubrics_metrics.description: "I love to speak out and declare my Mind clearly, when I am talking for the Good of my Country. I will not make my Court to an ill Man..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial stance: when writing in service of public good, candid criticism of corrupt or unworthy public figures is justified; the writer claims the right to name or denounce bad politicians rather than flatter them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by results (proof of the pudding)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Proof of the P-dd-ng is in the eating."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical maxim applied to political or public claims: the value or truth of something should be judged by its outcomes rather than by rhetoric or professions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkenness is a despicable and deforming vice
rubrics_metrics.description: "a drunken Man is a greater Monster than any that is to be found among all the Creatures which God has made; ... no Character which appears more despicable and deformed... than that of a Drunkard."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluative criterion: drunkenness marks a person's character as contemptible; the essay frames drunkenness as socially and ethically condemnable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcohol both reveals and produces mental faults
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wine makes every latent Seed sprout up in the Soul, and shew it self. It gives Fury to the Passions, and Force to those Objects which are apt to produce them... Wine heightens Indifference into Love, Love into Jealousy, and Jealousy into Madness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical/moral explanation of how intoxication alters behaviour and judgement; includes the counterpoint to Seneca's remark (that drunkenness only discovers faults): Addison argues it also occasions faults a man is not naturally subject to (examples: jealousy, violence, vanity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term cognitive harms of habitual drunkenness
rubrics_metrics.description: "it insensibly weakens the Understanding, impairs the Memory, and makes those Faults habitual which are produced by frequent Excesses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for assessing the vice's lasting damage: repeated indulgence produces permanent decline in faculties and entrenched bad habits; author promises to treat bodily and financial harms in a future paper (signalling an evidence-based moral case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish honest ambition from petty/empty ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: "As the Work I have engaged in, will not only consist of Papers of Humour and Learning, but... There is scarce a Man living who is not actuated by Ambition... when this Principle meets with an honest Mind and great Abilities, it does infinite Service... when a Man only thinks of distinguishing himself, without being thus qualified for it, he becomes a very pernicious or a very ridiculous Creature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criterion for ambition: judged positively when matched with ability and virtue; judged negatively when it leads to trivial feats or ostentation (examples of trivial accomplishments like whistling, walking on hands, or street tricks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation based on trivial feats is shallow and ridiculous
rubrics_metrics.description: "How many are there whose whole Reputation depends upon a Punn or a Quibble? ... Some tumble into Fame, others grow immortal by throwing themselves through a Hoop."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern for public esteem: fame rooted in ostentatious but trivial accomplishments signifies petty ambition; such reputation lacks substantive merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold account of being present with the Maker (evaluative conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: First: disconsolate if God's presence confers no benefit; Second: deplorable if presence is felt only as wrath; Third: happy if presence is perceived in mercy and loving-kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework for theological/moral evaluation of a person's spiritual condition; used to motivate moral practice and to distinguish types of religious experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to be 'sensible' of God's presence: watch thoughts and keep God's word
rubrics_metrics.description: "If we would be thus Happy, and thus Sensible of our Maker's Presence... we must keep such a Watch over all our Thoughts... by Prayer and Meditation, by Virtue and good Works, opens this Communication between God and his own Soul."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive criteria for moral/religious life: guard thoughts, practice prayer/meditation, virtue, and obedience to divine precepts as means to internal spiritual experience and consolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognising quacks: common signs and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: "Impudence and many Words are as necessary to these Itinerary Galens as a laced Hat or a Merry Andrew... printed Bills and Advertisements... provide themselves of Persons to attest the Cure... 'their Medicines are infallible, and never fail of Success'... most of the bills agree in one Expression 'with God's Blessing' they perform such and such Cures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristics to detect charlatanry: extravagant claims of infallibility, heavy advertising, manufactured testimonials (knights of the post), long inventories of remedies, invoking divine blessing as rhetorical cover. Anecdotal examples and parody of advertising practice illustrate the anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical heuristic: true cures would make practitioners prosperous and unnecessary advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: "had all these Advertisers arrived to that Skill they pretend to, they would have had no Need for so many Years successively to publish to the World the Place of their Abode..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test of credibility: if a remedy were genuinely effective it would obviate persistent self-promotion; persistent advertising is evidence against authenticity (illustrated by the Gout anecdote: a true healer would be in a coach-and-six).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributing success to divine favour can mask lack of efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: "I observe that most of the Bills agree in one Expression, viz. that (with God's Blessing) they perform such and such Cures: This Expression is certainly very proper and emphatical, for that is all they have for it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical note that invoking God's blessing is often rhetorical padding rather than substantive proof; readers should treat such invocations as a signal for skepticism rather than evidence of efficacy.
